turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Skip cabbage and broccoli, they make it taste bitter. And potato peels make it cloudy.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Once the bag's full, then what?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Tip it all into a big pot, cover with cold water and simmer gently for two to three hours. Don't let it boil hard.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Do I salt it?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Leave it unsalted. Then you can season whatever you use it in later.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: That's just like her. She'd be / pleased I'm finally doing it.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: I'm sure she would. It's a lovely habit to carry on.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Is it actually dangerous to leave cooked rice out overnight? My flatmate does it all the time.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: It can be. Rice can carry bacteria spores that survive cooking and multiply at room temperature.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: But he's never been sick.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Lots of people get lucky. It's still better to cool rice within an hour and put it in the fridge.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: How do you cool it that fast?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Spread it out on a plate or tray. It cools much quicker than in a deep pot.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: And reheating, is once enough / or can you do it again?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Just once, and make sure it's steaming hot all the way through.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My four year old won't eat anything green. Not even peas.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Very common at that age. Hiding veg in sauces can help, but so can letting him see the green stuff over and over without pressure.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Hiding where, though?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Blend spinach or courgette into a tomato pasta sauce. Grated carrot disappears in meatballs.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: He does love meatballs.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Perfect then. You could even let him roll them with you, kids are more likely to eat what they've made.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: And the not pressuring part? Because / honestly I've been begging.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Put a tiny bit of green on his plate and say nothing about it. Eat yours happily. It can take ten or fifteen tries before they accept something new.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Fifteen. Wow. Okay.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: It's slow, but it does work. Hang in there.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I don't drink, and this beef stew recipe wants a whole bottle of red wine. What can I use?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Beef stock works well, with a splash of balsamic or red wine vinegar to add a bit of tang.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: How much vinegar?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Start with a tablespoon or two. You want a little acidity, not a salad dressing.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Could I use grape juice?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: You could, mixed with stock. Pure juice would make it too sweet.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Okay, stock and a bit of balsamic then. Should I / add anything else to make it rich?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: A spoon of tomato paste, fried with the onions until it darkens, gives a lot of depth.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: How do I know when a steak is medium rare without cutting into it?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: The easiest way is a meat thermometer. You're looking for about fifty-five degrees Celsius in the middle.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: No thermometer. Is there a trick?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: There's the finger test. Press the steak, it should feel soft but springy, like the base of your thumb when you touch your thumb to your middle finger.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: That feels very vague.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: It is, honestly. It gets better with practice, but a cheap thermometer saves a lot of guessing.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Fine, I'll buy one. And then I just slice it straight away?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Let it rest for five minutes first. The juices settle back in, so they don't run all over the board.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Five minutes feels like forever / when you're hungry.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Make the salad while you wait. It's worth it.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Recipe says two tablespoons of fresh thyme. I only have dried.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Use about a third as much dried, so roughly two teaspoons.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Why less?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Dried herbs are more concentrated because the water's gone.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Does that work for all herbs?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: For woody ones like thyme, rosemary and oregano, yes. Soft herbs like basil or coriander lose a lot when dried, so they're not a great swap.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Good to know. When do I add it, at the start / or the end?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Dried herbs go in early so they have time to soften. Fresh soft herbs go in at the very end.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: So I got a slow cooker for my birthday. Apparently I'm now a person who owns a slow cooker.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Welcome to the easy life. Have you tried anything in it yet?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Nope. It's just sitting there looking judgmental.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Start with a pulled pork. Rub a shoulder with spices, put it on sliced onions, and cook it on low for eight hours.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Eight hours. Can I leave it on while I'm at work?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Yes, that's what they're for. Just make sure it's on a clear counter, away from anything that could fall on it.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: And it comes out / not dry, right? Because my last pork was like cardboard.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Slow cooking keeps it moist. Shred it with two forks and mix it with a little of the cooking juice.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Okay. Maybe the judgmental pot and I can be friends.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: I think you'll get along fine.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Do air fryers really cook chips as well as a deep fryer?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Not quite as crispy, but close, and with way less oil. Most people are happy with them.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: What's the trick for fresh potatoes?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Cut them evenly, soak them in cold water for half an hour, then dry them really well before tossing with a spoon of oil.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Why soak them?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: It washes off surface starch, so they crisp instead of going gummy.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Right. And how long / do they need in there?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: About twenty minutes at a high setting, shaking the basket halfway through. Don't overfill it or they'll steam.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I want to make green curry paste from scratch. Is it worth it, or should I just buy a jar?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Homemade is noticeably fresher and brighter. It's worth trying at least once.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: What goes in it?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Green chilies, lemongrass, galangal or ginger, garlic, shallots, coriander roots, lime zest, and a little shrimp paste.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Coriander roots? I've only ever seen the leaves.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Look for bunches with roots still on at an Asian grocer. The stems work too if you can't find them.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: And I just blend it all?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Yes, with a splash of oil. A pestle and mortar gives a better texture, but a blender is fine.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Does it keep? I'd rather make a big batch / so I'm not doing this every week.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: It keeps about a week in the fridge. Freeze the rest in an ice cube tray, then you can grab a portion whenever you want.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My dad was just diagnosed with type two diabetes and he lives with us. What should I change about dinners?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: I'm sorry to hear that. The big things are fewer refined carbs, more fiber, and smaller portions of rice, pasta and bread.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: He loves his rice though.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: He doesn't have to give it up. Try brown rice, or mix white rice with lentils, and fill half the plate with vegetables.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Okay. What about dessert?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Fresh fruit with yogurt is a good swap. A small piece of dark chocolate now and then is fine for most people.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Should I / talk to someone about a proper meal plan for him?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Yes, a dietitian would be a great idea. His doctor can usually refer him, and they'll tailor it to his medication.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Thanks, that's less scary than I thought.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Small changes go a long way. You're doing a good thing for him.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My grandma's coming over to teach me her dumplings and I want to impress her by prepping the filling. Pork and cabbage.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's a classic. Finely chop the cabbage, salt it and squeeze out the water before mixing it with the pork.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Why squeeze it?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Otherwise the filling gets watery and the dumplings tear when you fold them.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: What else goes in?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Ginger, spring onion, soy sauce, a little sesame oil and white pepper. Stir it in one direction until it turns sticky.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: One direction? That sounds like / something she would say.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: It's real advice. It helps the filling bind, so it stays juicy.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Okay, I'm doing that and hoping she doesn't redo it all.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Even if she adjusts it, she'll love that you tried.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I'm a nurse on night shifts. What's a decent thing to eat before I leave at seven in the evening?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Something balanced that won't make you sleepy. Think protein and slow carbs, like a chicken and bean wrap or an omelette with toast.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: And during the shift? I usually end up eating crisps at three in the morning.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Pack a small second meal, like a pot of soup or a grain salad. Light and easy to eat standing up.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I never have time to cook, though.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Make one big tray bake on your day off and portion it out. Roast vegetables, chickpeas and some chicken thighs keep well for four days.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Huh. That could actually work / if I'm not too tired on my day off.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Even an hour on Sunday afternoon covers most of the week. Your three in the morning self will thank you.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Caramelizing onions takes forever. Can I just turn the heat up?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: You can go a bit higher, but too much heat burns them before they go sweet.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: The recipe said ten minutes. It's been twenty-five.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's really common. Properly caramelized onions usually take forty minutes or more.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Seriously? Recipes lie?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Quite often about onions, yes. A pinch of salt helps them release water and soften faster.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: What about sugar?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: A little sugar speeds the browning, but it's not true caramelizing. Fine if you're in a hurry, though.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I'll keep going / I guess. My burger can wait.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My garden is drowning in cucumbers. Can I pickle them without canning equipment?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Yes, fridge pickles are easy. You just need jars, vinegar, water, salt, a little sugar and some dill.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: What ratio?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Equal parts vinegar and water, with about a tablespoon of salt and a teaspoon of sugar per cup of liquid.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Hot or cold?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Heat the liquid just until the salt dissolves, then pour it over the sliced cucumbers in the jars.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: And how long until they're ready?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: They're tasty after a day, and best after three or four. Keep them in the fridge and eat them within a month.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: A month, that's fine. We go through / a ridiculous amount of pickles.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then make a few jars with garlic or chili flakes too, for some variety.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Do you wash mushrooms or just brush them? My partner and I are literally arguing about this right now.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Ha. A quick rinse is fine, as long as you dry them right away and cook them soon after.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: So brushing isn't the only proper way?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Brushing works for lightly dirty ones. Mushrooms don't soak up as much water as people think from a short rinse.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I'm going to tell him you said I win.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: I'd call it a draw. Just don't leave them sitting in water.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Fine, a draw. And how do I get them / you know, brown and not soggy?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Hot pan, not too many at once, and salt them only after they've browned.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I'm cooking just for myself now, after twenty years of cooking for a family. It feels a bit pointless.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's a big change, and it makes sense that it feels strange. Cooking for one can still be a nice thing to do for yourself.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Everything I make lasts for days though.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: You could cook a full recipe and freeze single portions. Then you have homemade ready meals on tired evenings.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: That's sensible. What about things that don't freeze?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Try dishes that are naturally small, like an omelette, a quick pasta, or a piece of fish with some greens. Ten minutes and no leftovers.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I used to make fish for the kids every Friday. Maybe / I'll keep doing that, just smaller.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That sounds like a lovely way to keep the tradition. Treat yourself to a nice piece.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Just moved into my first flat. Which spices should I buy first? The shelf at the shop is overwhelming.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Start small. Black pepper, cumin, smoked paprika, chili flakes, dried oregano and cinnamon cover a lot of dishes.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Cinnamon for savory stuff?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Yes, a pinch in chili or a tagine is great. And of course for porridge.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: What about those big mixed jars, like curry powder?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Curry powder and garam masala are handy shortcuts. Buy small jars, though, spices lose their flavor after a year or so.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I'll get the basics then. Is it worth buying / whole ones and grinding them?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Eventually, maybe. For now, ground is perfectly fine.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Can I make fresh pasta without a pasta machine?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Definitely. You just need flour, eggs, a rolling pin and some patience.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: How much flour per egg?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Roughly a hundred grams of flour for each egg. Knead it for about ten minutes until it's smooth.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My arms are going to fall off.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Maybe a little. Let the dough rest for half an hour wrapped up, it gets much easier to roll after.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Then roll it super thin?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Thin enough that you can almost see your hand through it. Dust it with flour, roll it up loosely and slice it into ribbons.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: And cooking time? I'm guessing it's not / the same as dried pasta.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Much shorter, two or three minutes in salted boiling water. Taste one to check.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I'm hosting brunch and my hollandaise always splits. What am I doing wrong?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Usually the butter goes in too fast or the bowl gets too hot.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I'm doing it over a pan of simmering water.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Make sure the bowl isn't touching the water, and keep it at a gentle simmer. Add the melted butter in a very thin stream while whisking.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: And if it splits anyway, is it ruined?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: No. Put a fresh egg yolk in a clean bowl and slowly whisk the split sauce into it. It usually comes back.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Oh, that's a relief. Can I make it / an hour before people arrive?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: It's best fresh, but you can keep it warm in a thermos for about an hour.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: A thermos. That's genius.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: It's an old cafe trick. Enjoy the brunch.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: We're fasting this month and I cook iftar every night for six people. I'm running out of ideas.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's a lot of cooking. Do you want quick dishes, or things you can prepare during the afternoon?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Afternoon is fine, I'm home. But I'm tired by then.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then go for dishes that mostly cook unattended. A lentil soup to open the fast, then something like a baked chicken and rice dish.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: We already do lentil soup every single night. It's tradition.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then keep it, and change the mains. Stuffed peppers, a kofta tray bake, or a big pot of chickpea stew all work.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Kofta tray bake sounds good. Can I / make the meat mix the night before?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Yes, and it'll taste better for it. Keep it covered in the fridge and shape it in the afternoon.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Quick question. How do you get garlic smell off your hands?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Rub them on something stainless steel under cold water, like the side of the sink or a spoon. Then wash with soap.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: That sounds made up.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: It does, but plenty of people swear by it. Lemon juice and a little salt also help.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: And peeling garlic faster? I have twenty cloves to do.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Crush each clove lightly with the flat of your knife, the skin slips right off.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Twenty cloves for one dish. My girlfriend's mum / doesn't believe in subtle.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then she'll be very happy with you tonight.

option_sets.lead_in: I can't decide what to make for dinner on Saturday when my in-laws come over.
options: The first idea is a big roast chicken with potatoes and carrots, all in one tray in the oven.
Then there's homemade lasagna, which I could make the night before and just bake when they arrive.
And the last one is grilled salmon with a lemon sauce and a green salad, lighter but more last minute.
moshi_comment: The lasagna is the least stressful, since you can make it ahead and actually enjoy your guests. The roast chicken is a safe crowd pleaser too, but timing the oven can be tricky. The salmon is lovely, though cooking it at the last minute while people are chatting is a lot of pressure.

Do your in-laws have any favorite foods, or anything they don't eat? If not, I'd go with the lasagna so you're not stuck in the kitchen. The roast chicken would be my second pick, it's simple and everyone likes it.

option_sets.lead_in: I want to bake something for the office bake sale and I've got three ideas.
options: One is chocolate chip cookies, easy and quick, and I can make like four dozen in an hour.
Another option is a lemon drizzle cake, which looks nice but has to be sliced up on the day.
Or I could do brownies with a salted caramel swirl, a bit messier but people always go crazy for them.
moshi_comment: For a bake sale, the cookies are hard to beat, they're quick, cheap, and easy to sell one at a time. The brownies would probably sell out first, though, so they might be worth the mess. The lemon cake looks pretty, but slicing it on the day adds work.
How much time do you have the night before? If it's tight, go with the cookies. If you've got a free evening, the salted caramel brownies will likely be the big hit of the table.

option_sets.lead_in: My work friends want me to host a potluck and I've no clue what to make as the host.
options: I could do a huge pot of chili with all the toppings on the side, so people build their own bowls.
There's also a taco bar, which is fun, but it means warming tortillas all evening while people arrive.
Or a couple of big roasted trays, like sausages and vegetables, which basically cook themselves.
moshi_comment: The chili is my pick, it sits happily on the stove and people can help themselves whenever they turn up. The taco bar is the most fun, but you'd be stuck warming tortillas. The roasting trays are easy too, just less of a centerpiece.

If you want to actually mingle, go with the trays or the chili, since both look after themselves. The taco bar sounds great but keeps you tied to the stove. Between the two easy ones, chili feels more like a host dish.

option_sets.lead_in: I'm trying to get more vegetables into my week and I've got three plans in mind.
options: Plan A is a big soup on Sunday that I eat for lunch every day, mostly lentils, carrots and greens.
Plan B is sneaking veg into everything, like grated courgette in sauces and spinach in my eggs.
Plan C is a veg box delivery, which forces me to cook whatever turns up each week, even weird stuff.
moshi_comment: Plan B is the easiest to stick with because it doesn't change what you already eat. The Sunday soup is great but you might be bored by Thursday. The veg box is the most adventurous, and good if you like a challenge.

I'd combine them a little. Sneak veg into what you already cook, like in plan B, and make the soup only every other week. The box is great fun, but if you're busy, half of it might end up wilting in the fridge.

option_sets.lead_in: My daughter wants to help cook on Saturday and I need something a seven year old can do.
options: Homemade pizza, where she rolls the dough and picks her own toppings, though the kitchen will get covered in flour.
Maybe meatballs, she'd love squishing them, but raw meat and little hands make me a bit nervous.
Or fruit skewers with a yogurt dip, which is safe and quick but maybe not very exciting for her.
Possibly pancakes, she can stir and pour while I do the flipping at the stove.
moshi_comment: Pizza is the winner for a seven year old, she gets to make choices and it feels like her dinner. The pancakes are a close second. Meatballs are fine with hand washing, and the skewers might be over in five minutes.
I'd go with pizza and accept the flour. Kids remember the messy ones. Pancakes are a calmer backup, and the fruit skewers could be a nice little side job while the pizza bakes.

option_sets.lead_in: I'm cooking for my boyfriend's parents for the first time and I'm torn on the main course.
options: A chicken pie, which is homely and safe, and I can make the pastry the day before.
Paella, it's my best dish and it looks impressive, but his mum doesn't really like seafood.
A big lamb tagine with couscous, which smells amazing but I've only cooked it once before.
moshi_comment: The chicken pie is the safest bet, it's comforting and you can prep it ahead. The paella is your strongest dish, but a seafood problem is a real risk with his mum. The tagine sounds wonderful, though I'd rather not try a nearly new recipe on the big night.

Could you make the paella with chicken and chorizo instead of seafood? Then you get to show off your best dish. If not, I'd go with the pie and keep the tagine for another time when there's less pressure.
